A tuber is a swollen, fleshy underground part of a plant that stores food — mainly starch — for the plant to use later. Think of it as a natural underground food warehouse that the plant builds and fills up during the growing season, then draws from when conditions are harsh (cold winters, dry spells) or when it needs energy to sprout new growth.

The potato is the most famous example. When you dig up a potato plant, the round lumpy things you find underground are tubers. Each one is packed with starch.

Two reasons:

  1. Survival — The tuber acts as a reserve tank. When the above-ground plant dies back in winter or drought, the tuber stays dormant underground with all its stored energy intact. When conditions improve, it fuels the plant's regrowth.
  2. Reproduction — Tubers let the plant multiply vegetatively (without seeds). A single tuber, or even a piece of one, can grow into a whole new plant. This is why farmers plant potato chunks rather than seeds.

Botanically, there are two distinct types, depending on which part of the plant got swollen:

1. Stem tubers — These form from underground stems (or underground horizontal runners called stolons). The potato is the classic example. You can tell it's a modified stem because it has eyes — those small dimples on the surface. Each eye is actually a node (a spot on a stem where buds can form), and new shoots sprout from them. Other stem tubers: yam, Jerusalem artichoke, cyclamen.

2. Root tubers — These form from roots, not stems. Because they're roots, they don't have eyes/nodes from which shoots sprout. New plants form from the crown (the junction where the tuber meets the main stem above ground). Examples: sweet potato, cassava (the source of tapioca), and dahlia.

In everyday conversation, people often use "tuber" loosely for any starchy underground vegetable, without worrying about whether it's technically a stem tuber or root tuber. That's perfectly fine in casual use.
How a tuber is different from similar underground structures

Plants have several other underground storage structures, and they're often confused with tubers. Here's what sets each apart:

Bulb (onion, garlic, tulip) — A bulb is essentially a tightly packed bundle of thick, fleshy modified leaves wrapped around a tiny compressed stem at the base. If you cut an onion in half, you'll see those concentric layers — those are the leaves. A tuber, by contrast, is solid fleshy stem or root tissue, not layered leaves.

Corm (taro, crocus, gladiolus) — A corm looks similar to a stem tuber from the outside, but it is solid all the way through and is entirely consumed (used up) over one growing season as it fuels new growth, while a fresh corm forms above the old one. A stem tuber, on the other hand, persists and doesn't fully deplete itself.

Rhizome (ginger, turmeric, iris) — A rhizome is a modified stem too, but it grows horizontally underground rather than swelling up into a compact rounded mass. Ginger root is a good example — that knobby, elongated piece you use in cooking is a rhizome, not a tuber. Rhizomes spread laterally and are more elongated; tubers are more compact and rounded.

Taproot (carrot, radish, turnip, beet) — A taproot is simply the main central root of the plant, which has grown large and fleshy to store food. It's a single, continuous root growing downward. A root tuber, by contrast, is a swollen side root or adventitious root (a root that grows from an unusual location, like from the base of a stem), and there can be many of them on one plant (think of a dahlia plant's cluster of thick roots).

Outside of botany, tuber appears in anatomy and medicine to describe a rounded, bump-like projection or swelling on a bone or body structure. For example, the bony protrusion you feel when you sit on a hard surface is called the ischial tuberosity (from "tuber"). This meaning — a rounded lump — is actually the same underlying idea: something swollen and rounded. In medical and anatomical contexts, you'll see it used this way in technical descriptions.

A tuber is a swollen underground plant structure — either a modified stem or a modified root — that stores starch as a food reserve and enables the plant to survive harsh conditions and reproduce. Potatoes (stem tubers) and sweet potatoes (root tubers) are the best-known examples. It is distinct from bulbs (which are made of layered leaves), corms (which are used up each year), rhizomes (which grow horizontally), and taproots (which are the plant's primary downward-growing root).
